deviations.aspect: Exposure — no highlight rolloff; pure 2^EV gain into a hard clip
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Adobe documents Exposure as f-stop-equivalent ("+1.00 is similar to opening the aperture 1 stop", ±5.00 range), but the PV2012 implementation is explicitly not a pure linear gain: it is midtone-weighted and rolls the highlights off with a film-like shoulder instead of the sharp cutoff of a real exposure change. Highlight separation survives a positive Exposure push; ACR's baseline rendering also already contains a tone curve + white-point mapping even with every slider at 0. In the LR histogram the Exposure slider owns the *middle* fifth of the tonal range (hover order Blacks → Shadows → Exposure → Highlights → Whites), not the whole range.
deviations.our_behavior: Exposure is a pure additive shift in EV space — `let x = x0 + t.exposure` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:126), so output = Y·2^EV exactly for every pixel, with no shoulder anywhere. The only thing that stops it is the hard `clamp(c, 0, 1)` in the sRGB encode (Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Common.metal:22, applied at Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Output.metal:9). Measured consequence: Exposure +1.00 maps every input above linear Y = 0.50 (sRGB 73.5%, 187/255) to pure white; Exposure +2.00 does the same to everything above Y = 0.25 (sRGB 53.7%, 137/255) — i.e. anything brighter than a light midtone. Nothing in the pipeline ever compresses toward white.
deviations.proposed_fix: Add an always-on display shoulder at the very end of `evaluateEV` (ToneCurve.swift:123-134), i.e. after the five control deltas are summed, mapping y → soft-clip with the knee below display white: `let W = log2(1/0.18) = 2.474; let k = 1.2; if y > k { y = k + (W - k) * (1 - exp(-(y - k)/(W - k))) }`. Monotone, C¹ at the knee, asymptotes exactly at linear 1.0 so nothing ever clips from tone alone, and it is one branch in one CPU function (the LUT carries it to the GPU; the maskable path in Tone.metal is unaffected because it runs on already-shouldered output). Accept that this retires the "all sliders zero == exact identity" invariant that ToneCurveTests currently relies on — LR's zero is not linear either. Optionally also make Exposure's own weight taper above the shoulder knee if a closer midtone weighting is wanted, but the shoulder alone fixes the visible failure.

deviations.aspect: Contrast — σ = 2.5 EV is wider than the entire visible highlight headroom, so Contrast alone blows the whites
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Adobe: "Increases or decreases image contrast, mainly affecting midtones." Structurally LR's contrast is a display-referred S-curve pivoted around mid-grey with the endpoints pinned: the darkest tone stays at its level and the brightest tone below white stays below white, exactly like the Medium/Strong Contrast point-curve presets whose endpoints are fixed at (0,0) and (100,100). Contrast +100 in LR steepens midtones and compresses toward the ends; it does not promote a light grey to paper white.
deviations.our_behavior: `contrastDeltaEV` is an odd Gaussian bump `c·0.55·x·exp(−x²/2·2.5²)` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:78-83, constants at :30-31; GPU twin at Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Tone.metal:26-27, 44-47). Its peak displacement is at x = ±σ = ±2.5 EV, but display white is only +2.474 EV above the 0.18 pivot — so inside the visible range the bump is monotonically *increasing* and never turns back toward the endpoint. Measured at Contrast +100: linear 0.36 (sRGB 63%) → 0.51; linear 0.50 (sRGB 73.5%) → 0.80; linear 0.595 (sRGB 79.5%, 203/255) → exactly 1.0. Everything above 79.5% grey is clipped to pure white by Contrast alone. Peak displacement is 0.834 EV. Symmetrically, Contrast −100 pulls display white down a full stop (2.474 → 1.64 EV, linear 0.56) — a "midtone" control moving the white point by a stop.
deviations.proposed_fix: Two constants plus the shoulder from the Exposure item. Set `contrastSigma` ≈ 1.2 EV and `contrastGain` ≈ 0.40 (ToneCurve.swift:30-31 and Tone.metal:26-27 must move together — ToneDeltaTests compares them). That puts the peak displacement at ±1.2 EV (linear 0.41 / 0.078), i.e. squarely in the midtones as documented, with ±0.16 EV left at display white instead of ±0.83 EV, and the shoulder absorbs the remainder. Slope at the pivot drops from 1.55 to 1.40 at +100, which is closer to LR's Strong Contrast preset anyway. If a truly endpoint-pinned S-curve is wanted later, evaluate contrast on the display-referred signal with pivot 0.5 (effort M) — but the two constants remove the visible blowout.

deviations.aspect: Highlights / Shadows — dead band through the midtones and both ramps sit ~1 EV too far out (KNOWN ISSUE: confirmed and quantified)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: LR's Highlights/Shadows build a soft mask that peaks in its zone and tapers rather than cutting off: brightening shadows "has the greatest effect on the darkest shadows, tapering off to a minimal effect on the highlights and vice versa" — a taper, not a dead band. Step-wedge observation of the Highlights slider: "the entire curve starts moving to the left, and while the high values move faster, the low values also get somewhat compressed", i.e. mid and low tones do move. Best available extent data: the LR histogram is divided into five draggable regions in the order Blacks → Shadows → Exposure → Highlights → Whites over a 0–100% luminance display scale. Taking them as equal fifths and decoding sRGB against a 0.18 pivot gives Shadows ≈ −2.44…−0.44 EV (centre ≈ −1.4 EV), Exposure ≈ −0.44…+0.82 EV (straddling middle grey), Highlights ≈ +0.82…+1.75 EV (centre ≈ +1.3 EV), Whites ≈ +1.75…+2.47 EV, Blacks below −2.44 EV (centre ≈ −4.2 EV). So LR's Highlights and Shadows peak roughly ±1.3–1.4 EV from middle grey and overlap the Exposure region on the way in.
deviations.our_behavior: `highlightsDeltaEV` / `shadowsDeltaEV` use `smootherstep(0.25, 4.0, ±x) · 1.2 EV` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:88-100, constants at :34-38; GPU twin Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Tone.metal:28-31, 48-55). Weight is exactly 0 for |x| < 0.25 EV and reaches 50% only at |x| = 2.125 EV — inside LR's *Whites/Blacks* territory, not its Highlights/Shadows zone. Measured at ±100: middle grey moves 0.000 EV; at LR's Highlights-zone centre (+1.3 EV, linear 0.44, sRGB 70%) only 0.165 EV; at LR's Shadows-zone centre (−1.4 EV, sRGB 30%) only 0.206 EV; at +1.0 EV a mere 0.070 EV. Full authority (1.2 EV) is not reached until |x| = 4 EV, which on the shadow side is deep inside LR's Blacks region and on the highlight side is 1.5 stops above anything the output transform can display. Net effect: Highlights −100 + Shadows +100 — the classic dynamic-range-compression move — leaves the whole −1…+1 EV core of the picture essentially untouched, so the image does not flatten the way it does in LR, and the two controls read as much weaker and much "further out" than their LR namesakes.
deviations.proposed_fix: Change the ramp endpoints and the range, in both the Swift and the MSL copy (they are compared by ToneDeltaTests). Concretely: highlights `smootherstep(−1.0, +3.5, x)`, shadows `smootherstep(−1.0, +3.5, −x)`, `highlightRange = shadowRange = 1.8 EV` — i.e. ToneCurve.swift:34-38 becomes `highlightRange/shadowRange = 1.8`, `highlightRamp = (-1.0, 3.5)`, `shadowRamp = (1.0, -3.5)` (kept in its negated storage convention), and Tone.metal:28-31 becomes `kToneHighlightRange/kToneShadowRange = 1.8f`, `kToneRampLo = -1.0f`, `kToneRampHi = 3.5f`. That puts 50% weight at ±1.25 EV (vs LR's ±1.3/−1.4 EV zone centres), gives 0.138 EV of reach at middle grey at ±100 (nonzero, and it cancels exactly when Highlights −100 and Shadows +100 are combined), 0.585 EV at the bottom of LR's Highlights zone and 1.65 EV at display white. Peak slope of the ramp is 1.875/4.5 × 1.8 = 0.75 per EV; combined with the retuned contrast (≤0.09 at that x) the monotonicity budget still closes at ≈0.84 < 1, **provided** whites/blacks stop contributing additive slope (see the Whites and Blacks items). Re-run ToneCurveTests.testMonotonicUnderRandomCombos after the change.

deviations.aspect: Whites — effectively inert: the ramp lives 2 EV above anything the display can show
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Adobe: "Whites — Adjusts white clipping. Drag to the left to reduce highlight clipping. Drag to the right to increase highlight clipping." It is *the* white-point control; users report that a single unit (Whites −1) is enough to make the red clipping overlay disappear, and Alt/Option-dragging it shows a dedicated clipping-threshold view. Its histogram region is the top fifth, ≈ +1.75…+2.47 EV relative to middle grey (centre ≈ +2.1 EV).
deviations.our_behavior: `whitesDeltaEV` = `w · 1.5 EV · smootherstep(1.0, 7.5, x)` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:105-109, constants :41-43). 50% weight lands at +4.25 EV — 1.8 stops *above* display white (+2.474 EV), i.e. on tones the output transform has already clamped to 255. Measured at Whites ±100: display white moves by only ±0.121 EV (±8.7% linear); linear 0.72 (sRGB 86.5%) moves ±0.043 EV; linear 0.60 (sRGB 80%) moves ±0.019 EV. Effectively a no-op slider in the visible range, and by construction it can never create or remove clipping — the tone curve's only clip is the output clamp, which Whites can barely reach.
deviations.proposed_fix: Take Whites out of the additive-EV sum and make it a white-point rescale in the CPU curve, which is both LR-like and frees the slope budget the Highlights fix needs. In `evaluateLinear`/`makeLUT` (ToneCurve.swift:181-225) pre-scale before the EV curve: `Y ← Y / whitePoint` with `whitePoint = exp2(-1.2 · whites/100)` (Whites +100 → white point drops to 0.44 of scene white, so the top 1.2 stops clip against the output clamp; Whites −100 → white point rises, pulling clipped tones back below 1.0). Delete `whitesRange`/`whitesRamp`/`whitesDeltaEV`. Whites is not maskable, so nothing in Tone.metal changes and the shader's `Y'/Y` ratio is unaffected. If you'd rather keep the additive shape, the minimum change is `whitesRamp = (0.8, 3.4)` (50% at +2.1 EV, matching LR's zone centre) with `whitesRange` reduced to ~0.8 EV to stay inside the slope budget — but that still never clips.

deviations.aspect: Blacks — never reaches zero, so the black point cannot be set (placement is fine, clipping is not)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Adobe, verbatim: "Blacks (PV2012) — Adjusts black clipping. Drag to the left to increase black clipping (map more shadows to pure black). Drag to the right to reduce shadow clipping." Blacks −100 genuinely crushes tones to RGB 0; the histogram's left clipping indicator lights up and Alt/Option-dragging gives a black-threshold view. Setting the black point this way is a core B&W move (Zone-system black placement, "there must be a true black in the print").
deviations.our_behavior: `blacksDeltaEV` = `b · 1.5 EV · smootherstep(1.0, 7.5, −x)` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:113-117, constants :42-44). Zone *placement* is actually good — 50% weight at −4.25 EV vs LR's Blacks-region centre ≈ −4.17 EV — but the maximum authority is a bounded −1.5 EV, so nothing ever becomes zero. A pixel at 10/255 (linear 0.00335, x ≈ −5.75 EV) at Blacks −100 gets 1.28 EV of darkening → linear 0.00138 → 6/255, not 0. At sRGB 20% (x = −2.44 EV) the move is only 0.114 EV. Consequences: the Blacks slider cannot produce a true black, the histogram's shadow-clip counter (min channel ≤ 0.5/255, GrayroomCore/README.md "Output transform") can never be triggered by it, and an Alt-drag black-threshold workflow is impossible to build on this curve. README.md:100-103 and :526 already flag this as deliberate.
deviations.proposed_fix: Same trick as Whites — move Blacks out of the additive-EV sum into a linear-domain pedestal applied before the log, in `evaluateLinear`/`makeLUT` only (ToneCurve.swift:181-225): `Y ← max(0, Y - p) / (1 - p)` with `p = 0.02 · max(0, -blacks)/100` for negative Blacks (2% of white ≈ 3.5 stops below middle grey at −100, which brackets LR's Blacks region), and `Y ← Y·(1-p) + p` with `p = 0.02 · max(0, blacks)/100` for positive Blacks (a lift that removes existing clipping). Delete `blacksRange`/`blacksRamp`/`blacksDeltaEV`. Monotonicity survives as *non-strict*: `makeLUT`'s running-max pass (ToneCurve.swift:209-215) already tolerates flat runs, and the kernel's `rgb * (Yp / Y)` at ToneCurve/Tone.metal:104 is safe with `Yp = 0` because the `Y <= 1e-9` branch guards the divisor. Blacks is not maskable, so Tone.metal needs no change. The one test to relax is the "strictly increasing / min slope > 0.05" assertion in ToneCurveTests — it must become "non-decreasing, strictly increasing above the black point".

deviations.aspect: Highlight recovery does not desaturate — tone stage is exactly ratio-preserving
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Pulling Highlights far down in LR visibly desaturates the recovered area; the recovery works per channel and converges toward neutral as channels run out of data, which is why recovered skies/clouds go pale and why the standard remedy is to add +8…+12 Saturation back with a local mask. Jim Kasson's measurements show detail remaining recoverable ~1.5 EV past clipping but with pronounced colour change over that range.
deviations.our_behavior: The tone kernel is a pure luminance remap: `outRGB = rgb * (Yp / Y)` (Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Tone.metal:104), and GrayroomCore/README.md states the intent explicitly — "Channel ratios — and therefore hue and HSV saturation — are untouched by construction", asserted by `testTonePreservesRatiosNoHueShift`. So Highlights −100 changes brightness and nothing else, and individual channels can stay far above 1.0 while luminance is brought back in range. This matters specifically for B&W because the mixer term is saturation-weighted (`gray = Y·(1 + Σ w_band(hue)·slider·sat)`, README "B&W mix"): a highlight region that LR would have neutralised during recovery stays fully saturated here, so e.g. a recovered blue sky responds far more strongly to the Blue mixer slider in Grayroom than in LR, and the same edit ported from LR lands in a different place.
deviations.proposed_fix: In the tone kernel, blend the result toward neutral in proportion to how much a channel is being pulled back from clipping: after computing `Yp`, take `float over = clamp(max(rgb.r, max(rgb.g, rgb.b)) / max(Y, 1e-6) * (Yp / Y) - 1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f);` and `outRGB = mix(rgb * (Yp / Y), float3(Yp), desatStrength * over)` with `desatStrength ≈ 0.6`. Cheap, monotone in luminance, and keeps the identity early-out. If the exact-ratio golden test is worth preserving, gate the desaturation on `highlights < 0` only, which is where LR's behaviour is visible.

deviations.aspect: Highlights / Shadows are a global 1-D curve; LR's are edge-aware
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Eric Chan (Adobe), on building the PV2012 Highlights/Shadows/Clarity sliders: the team "had been exploring various algorithms that used edges to modify various tones, but they were incredibly slow" — initially about a minute per megapixel, then ~8 seconds per file, before being optimised to near real time. That cost profile is only explicable for a spatially adaptive (edge-aware / local-contrast-preserving) operator, and it is why LR's Shadows +100 opens the shadows without visibly flattening local contrast in them, and why extreme settings can produce faint halos.
deviations.our_behavior: Highlights and Shadows are pure point functions of luminance, evaluated once into a 1-D LUT (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:88-100 and :205-225) and looked up per pixel (Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Tone.metal:88-100). A global curve that lifts shadows necessarily compresses local contrast within them by the local slope of the curve, so a Grayroom Shadows +100 looks flatter and "greyer" in the shadows than the LR equivalent for the same amount of lift; it also cannot produce halos, which is the tell users look for.
deviations.proposed_fix: No small fix — this is architectural. The cheap approximation, and the one that reuses machinery already in the repo: derive a blurred/edge-preserving guide from the clarity stage's Gaussian pyramid (Stages/ClarityStage.swift already builds one on log-luminance) and drive the highlight/shadow zone weights from the *guide* luminance rather than the pixel luminance, then apply the resulting EV offset to the pixel. That converts the point curve into a base-layer tone map with the detail layer passed through, which is the standard way to get LR-like shadow opening without flattening. Only worth doing after the ramp/endpoint items above land, since it inherits their constants.

deviations.aspect: Whites / Blacks are not available per mask
deviations.lightroom_behavior: LR Classic's mask adjustment set (Tone sub-panel) includes Whites and Blacks alongside Exposure, Contrast, Highlights and Shadows — the research inventory lists "Temp, Tint, Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Texture, Clarity, Dehaze…" for every mask type. Setting a local black point (e.g. crushing a distracting background) is a routine B&W move.
deviations.our_behavior: `MaskAdjustments` carries only exposure/contrast/highlights/shadows/clarity (Sources/GrayroomCore/Masks/Mask.swift:72-96), and the maskable curve `toneDeltaEV` deliberately implements three components (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:143-150, documented at :141-142; GPU twin Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Tone.metal:41-57). A user who reaches for a local Blacks in Grayroom finds the slider missing.
deviations.proposed_fix: Add `whites`/`blacks` to `MaskAdjustments` and to the parameter textures. The blocker is that paramsA is a single rgba16Float already carrying four channels (README "Parameter accumulation"), so this needs a second rgba16Float (or packing the existing r16Float clarity map into a wider texture). Worth deferring until the global Whites/Blacks semantics are settled — if they become a linear white-point/pedestal (see those items) the per-pixel version is a different shape from the current additive-EV components and should be designed once, not twice.

deviations.aspect: Tone controls are a fixed curve; LR's Basic tone controls are image-adaptive
deviations.lightroom_behavior: PV2012+ Basic tone controls are image-adaptive: the same numeric slider values produce different curves on different images because the algorithm reads the image's tonal distribution, which is why Adobe's engineers recommend adjusting the Basic sliders top-down in order and why the sliders interact ("if settings are not kept equal and opposite, the image data levels shift left or right in the histogram, causing a much stronger interaction with all other control areas").
deviations.our_behavior: `ToneCurve.makeLUT` is a pure function of the six slider values (Sources/GrayroomCore/Stages/ToneCurve.swift:205-225) — no image statistics enter it. Two images given identical sliders get identical curves. User-visible effect: sidecar values copied from an LR edit will not reproduce that edit across a set of images, and slider values are not transferable between a dark frame and a bright one the way LR users expect.
deviations.proposed_fix: Probably don't. Adaptivity is the single most-complained-about property of LR's Basic panel and a deterministic curve is arguably the better design for a personal tool. If any adaptivity is wanted, the cheapest LR-shaped version is to place the Highlights/Shadows ramp midpoints from the image's log-luminance percentiles (e.g. 95th/5th) rather than at fixed EV offsets — one histogram pass, already available from the histogram tap, feeding two constants into `makeLUT`. Record the decision in README's "Known limitations" either way; today it is undocumented.

ANSWER TO QUESTION 5 (max ranges vs LR's reach at ±100). The *nominal* ranges are in the right ballpark but the *effective* reach inside the visible range is 5–10× too small, because the ramps are placed outside it. Display white sits at only +2.474 EV above the 0.18 pivot, and everything above it is clamped by the sRGB encode.

  control     nominal max   weight at LR's zone centre   effective ΔEV at ±100 there
  Highlights  1.2 EV        13.8% at +1.3 EV             0.165 EV
  Shadows     1.2 EV        17.2% at −1.4 EV             0.206 EV
  Whites      1.5 EV         8.0% at display white       0.121 EV
  Blacks      1.5 EV        47.7% at −4.17 EV            0.715 EV (and never reaches 0)

Blacks is the one whose *placement* is right (50% weight at −4.25 EV vs LR's Blacks-region centre ≈ −4.17 EV); its problem is purely that it cannot clip. Whites is the worst: 50% weight at +4.25 EV, i.e. 1.8 stops above anything the output transform can display. Exposure ±5 and per-mask exposure ±4 both match LR exactly (EditState.swift:132, Mask.swift:81) — no deviation there.

HOW LR'S ZONE EXTENTS WERE DERIVED. Adobe publishes no numbers. The best available anchor is the LR histogram's five draggable regions in the documented order Blacks → Shadows → Exposure → Highlights → Whites over a 0–100% luminance scale. Treating them as equal fifths and decoding sRGB against a 0.18 pivot gives: Blacks < −2.44 EV (centre ≈ −4.17), Shadows −2.44…−0.44 (centre ≈ −1.4), Exposure −0.44…+0.82 (straddles middle grey), Highlights +0.82…+1.75 (centre ≈ +1.3), Whites +1.75…+2.47. The equal-fifths assumption is *not* confirmed by any source I could find (glensmith.co.uk and the JPEGmini/Fstoppers histogram write-ups name the five regions but give no boundaries), so treat the ±0.2 EV of those centres as unverified. Everything downstream of it is marked "community-measured" or "inferred" accordingly.

ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT WORTH SURFACING TO THE MAINTAINER. The curve's design — five additive EV bumps with a hard invariant Σ|dΔ/dx| < 1 so the curve is *strictly* increasing (README "Monotonicity") — is what forces the current constants to be weak and far out. There is a fixed slope budget of 1.0 shared between five controls; you cannot give any one of them LR-like authority without taking it from the others. The two structural moves that free the budget, and which the Whites/Blacks fixes above both use, are: (a) take Whites and Blacks out of the additive sum entirely and implement them as a linear-domain white-point/black-pedestal in `makeLUT` — they are not maskable, so this touches ToneCurve.swift only and Tone.metal not at all; and (b) relax "strictly increasing with min slope > 0.05" to "non-decreasing, with permitted flat runs at the clipped ends", which `makeLUT`'s existing running-max pass (ToneCurve.swift:209-215) already supports and which is what LR itself does. Do (a) and (b) first, then the Highlights/Shadows ramp retune closes at a comfortable 0.84 slope budget.

RECOMMENDED ORDER OF ATTACK: Blacks pedestal + Whites white-point (unblocks everything, small, CPU-only) → Highlights/Shadows ramp constants (one-line changes in two files, must move together or ToneDeltaTests fails) → Contrast σ/gain → display shoulder for Exposure. The first four are all S/M and together close the large majority of the visible gap. The edge-aware Highlights/Shadows and per-mask Whites/Blacks are the only L-effort items and neither is needed to make the panel feel Lightroom-like.

THINGS I CHECKED AND FOUND *NOT* TO BE DEVIATIONS (so they don't get re-litigated): the CPU/GPU highlight-shadow mirroring is consistent (ToneCurve.swift:99 `smootherstep(0.25, 4.0, -x)` matches Tone.metal:54); exposure is applied before the zone weights in both, matching LR's ordering; the 0.18 contrast pivot matches LR's mid-grey pivot; Rec.709 luma weights and the 4096-entry LUT resolution are implementation detail with no visible consequence; slider clamping ranges match LR's UI.
